questions.q: What is the scope of a name?
questions.explain: Scope is where a name exists. Outside its scope, using the name throws a ReferenceError. It is about where, not about the type or the memory.
options: The type of value the name holds
The part of the program where the name can be used
The file the name was first used in
How long the value stays in memory

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: prefix only exists inside makeTitle. Reading it outside throws a ReferenceError ("I do not know this name"), not undefined.

questions.q: Why is it a good thing that a variable inside a function cannot be used outside it?
questions.explain: Each function keeps its own names. Two functions can both have a prefix variable and never clash. That is what makes large programs manageable.
options: It makes the program run faster
Two functions can use the same variable name without disturbing each other
It stops the function from being called twice

questions.q: A name is declared with let inside the body of an if. What kind of scope does it have?
questions.explain: let and const inside { } have block scope: they exist only inside that block. Module scope is for names at the top level of a file.

questions.q: You declare const appName = "Tasks"; at the top level of app.js. Where can it be used?
questions.explain: Top-level names have module scope. All code in that file sees them. Other files cannot, unless the file exports them. People often loosely call this "global", but it is not truly global.
options: Anywhere in any file of the project
By every function in app.js; other files only if app.js exports it
Only in the first function below it

questions.q: Which of these lives in the truly global scope?
questions.explain: The global scope holds what JavaScript provides, such as console, Math and JSON. You can reach it anywhere, also through globalThis. Your own top-level names are module scope.
options: A const at the top of your file
A variable declared in a loop

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: openCount belongs to the function and note to the if block, so outside they are unknown. typeof is the one place where an unknown name does not throw: it gives "undefined".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: var ignores blocks: it belongs to the whole function (or module), so a leaks out of the if. let stays inside its block, so b is unknown outside.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The functions run after the loop has finished. With var there is only one i for the whole loop, and by then it is 3. All three functions read that same variable.
options:
var: undefined
var: undefined
var: undefined

questions.q: The same loop, but with let. What does this print?
questions.explain: With let, every turn of the loop gets its own j. Each function remembers its own copy through a closure, so they print 0, 1 and 2.

questions.q: JavaScript uses lexical scope. What decides which outer variables a function can see?
questions.explain: "Lexical" means "about the written text". A function sees the scopes around the place it is written, not the scopes of whoever calls it.
options: Where the function is written in the file
The order in which functions are called
Whether it is an arrow function or not

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: show is written at the top level, so it looks up label in the module scope. The label inside caller is invisible to it, even though caller is the one calling it.

questions.q: Code inside a function uses the name limit. In which order does JavaScript look for it?
questions.explain: Scopes sit inside each other like boxes. The lookup starts in the innermost box and moves outwards to the module and global scope. The first match wins.
options: Global scope first, then outwards to the function
Only the current function, then it gives up
The current scope first, then each surrounding scope outwards; the first match wins
The scope of the function that called it, then the global scope

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The inner let count shadows the outer one: it is a new variable that hides the outer name. Changing it does not touch the outer count, which stays 10.

questions.q: You notice two variables called user, one in a function and one in a block inside it. What does the lesson advise?
questions.explain: Shadowing works, but a reader easily mixes up which user is meant. Give them different names.
options: Leave it: shadowing is the normal style
Rename one of them, because shadowing is legal but confusing
Move both to the global scope

questions.q: What is a closure?
questions.explain: A function carries its surrounding scope with it. Even after the outer function has returned, the inner function can still read and change the outer variables. Function plus remembered variables = closure.
options: A function that has finished running
A function together with the outer variables it remembers
A block that closes a scope with }
A way to stop a function from being called again

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call to makeCounter creates a new count. nextTaskId and nextUserId each keep their own, so the user counter starts again at 1.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A closure keeps a link to the variable, not a snapshot of its value. When describe runs, it reads the current value of mode.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: items is a variable inside createStore, not a property of the returned object. Only add can reach it through the closure, so store.items is undefined. That is private state.

questions.q: In the lesson's task store, list() returns tasks.map((t) => ({ ...t })) instead of tasks. Why?
questions.explain: Returning the real array (or the real task objects) would let any caller change private data, for example rename a task. Copies keep the store the only place where tasks change.
options: Because map is faster than returning the array
So callers get copies: changing them cannot change the tasks inside the store
Because returning a closure variable throws an error
So the list is sorted by id

questions.q: Why is it useful that the task store keeps nextId inside a closure instead of on the returned object?
questions.explain: Only the store's own functions can reach nextId. Outside code cannot reset or change it, so every id stays unique.
options: It lets callers change the ids when they need to
No caller can set it back to 1 and create duplicate ids

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A function declaration is hoisted ready to call, so you can call it above the line where it is written. This is the only hoisting the lesson says to rely on.
options: TypeError: double is not a function

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A var is created before the code runs and holds undefined until its line runs. It does not fail, which hides the mistake.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: limit exists (it was hoisted), but its line has not run yet. Using it in this temporal dead zone throws "Cannot access … before initialization". "is not defined" would mean the name does not exist at all.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An arrow function stored in a const follows the const rule, not the function declaration rule. Before its line it is in the temporal dead zone, so calling it throws a ReferenceError.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call the temporal dead zone helpful?
questions.explain: var quietly gives undefined, and the bug shows up somewhere else later. let and const throw right where the mistake is.
options: Using a name too early fails loudly at the exact spot, instead of quietly giving undefined
It lets you use a variable before you declare it
It hides errors from the user

questions.q: What is the difference between "x is not defined" and "Cannot access 'x' before initialization"?
questions.explain: Both are ReferenceErrors. "is not defined" means the name is unknown in every surrounding scope. "before initialization" means you used a let, const or class in its temporal dead zone.
options: They mean the same thing in different Node.js versions
The first: no scope has a name x. The second: x exists, but its declaration line has not run yet
The first is for const, the second for var
The first is a TypeError, the second a SyntaxError

questions.q: Why do two calls of the same function never share their local variables?
questions.explain: Every call creates a new execution context: which function runs, its own locals and parameters, and where to return to. So each call has fresh variables.
options: JavaScript copies the whole function before each call
Each call gets its own execution context, with its own local variables and parameters
Local variables are deleted before the function starts
Only one call of a function can run per program

questions.q: a calls b, and b calls c. What does this print?
questions.explain: Calling a function pushes it on the call stack, and the caller waits. c finishes first, then b carries on, then a. The last function called is the first to return.
options: done a start, b start, c, b end, a end
done a start, a end, b start, b end, c
done c, b start, b end, a start, a end
done a start, b start, c, a end, b end

questions.q: While validate runs inside save, which runs inside handleRequest, what are save and handleRequest doing?
questions.explain: Only the context on top of the stack runs. The functions below are paused, waiting for the answer, and carry on from where they stopped.
options: They have finished and been removed
They run at the same time as validate
They wait underneath on the call stack for validate to return

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: countDown has no base case, so it calls itself thousands of times until the call stack is full. JavaScript then throws a RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

questions.q: What does a recursive function need so it does not overflow the stack?
questions.explain: A base case, such as if (n === 0) return "lift off";, ends the recursion. try/catch only catches the crash, it does not fix it.
options: A base case: a condition where it stops calling itself
To be written as an arrow function
A var counter at the top of the file

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: markDone follows the reference to the object on the heap and changes it. replace only points its own parameter at a new object; the variable outside still points at the old one.

questions.q: Where do objects, arrays and functions live, and what does a variable hold?
questions.explain: Objects live on the heap. A variable only holds a reference, which is why two variables can point at the same object.
options: On the call stack; the variable holds a full copy
On the heap; the variable holds a reference to them
In the file; the variable holds the line number
In the global scope; the variable holds their name

questions.q: A server keeps a module-level array cache and pushes every response into it, never removing anything. What happens over time?
questions.explain: The garbage collector only removes objects nobody can reach. A module-level array stays reachable, so it is a memory leak. Use a cache with a size limit and expiry, like @zudojs/cache.
options: The garbage collector frees the oldest entries on its own
Memory keeps growing, because everything in the array stays reachable forever
Node.js throws a RangeError after 1000 entries
Nothing, because arrays are stored on the stack

questions.q: A stack trace lists several at … lines. How should you read it?
questions.explain: The top of the stack is where it failed. Lines starting with node:internal are Node.js itself, so skip them. The cause is often a step or two further down, in a caller.
options: Start at the bottom line, because that is where the error happened
Read only the lines that start with node:internal
Start at the top, find the first line in your own code, then walk down to where the bad value came from
Ignore it and read only the error name

questions.q: The trace says TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'city') at return user.address.city;. What does it mean?
questions.explain: The message names the property that was being read (city) from something that was undefined. So the value before .city, user.address, is missing.
options: user.address is undefined, so reading city from it failed
The file has a syntax error on that line

questions.q: The lesson suggests a safer way to read a city when data may be missing. What does this print?
questions.explain: ?. stops and gives undefined when the value before it is missing, instead of throwing. ?? then replaces undefined with "unknown". For id 3, user itself is undefined, and ?. handles that too.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: inner is written inside outer, so it finds outer's level first, and keeps it through its closure even after outer returned. The module's level never changed.

questions.q: Finish makeCounter(start). It returns a function that adds 1 to a private count (starting at start) and returns the new count. The two counters must not share their count. The program should print 11 12 1.
questions.explain: Keep the count in a let inside makeCounter and return an arrow function that changes it. Each call to makeCounter creates its own count.

questions.q: Write limit(fn, max). It returns a new function that calls fn at most max times; after that it returns "limit reached". Use a closure to count. The program should print welcome ada, welcome ada, then limit reached, each on its own line.
questions.explain: A calls variable in the closure remembers how many times the function ran. Check it before calling fn. This is the idea behind rate limiting login routes.
questions.expected:
welcome ada
welcome ada
limit reached

questions.q: This sumTo overflows the stack because it has no base case. Add one, so it returns 0 for n of 0 or less. The program should print 10 and then 0.
questions.explain: if (n <= 0) return 0; stops the recursion. Using <= instead of === also stops it for negative numbers.

questions.q: Finish createTaskStore(). Keep the tasks array and the next id private in the closure. add(title) adds { id, title } with ids 1, 2, 3…; count() returns how many tasks there are. The program should print 2 undefined.
questions.explain: Declare tasks and nextId inside the function and return only the methods. The array is not a property of the returned object, so store.tasks is undefined.

questions.q: This loop saves three functions, but they all print 3. Change the loop so each function remembers its own number. The program should print 0 1 2.
questions.explain: With var there is one i for the whole loop. With let, each turn gets its own i, and each function's closure keeps its own value.

questions.q: Write once(fn). It returns a function that calls fn the first time and remembers the result; every later call returns that saved result without calling fn again. The program should print setup, then ready ready.
questions.explain: Two closure variables do the job: called remembers whether fn ran, result keeps its answer. Both stay private between calls.

questions.q: Write a recursive factorial(n): factorial(n) is n * factorial(n - 1), and factorial(1) (and anything below 1) is 1. The program should print 120 1.
questions.explain: The base case if (n <= 1) return 1; stops the recursion. Without it, the calls go on into negative numbers until the stack overflows.

questions.q: Finish cityOf(id) so it never throws: return the user's city, or "unknown" when the user or the address is missing. The program should print London unknown unknown.
questions.explain: user?.address?.city gives undefined instead of throwing when something is missing, and ?? "unknown" supplies the fallback.

questions.q: Write makeTotal(). It returns an object with add(amount), which adds to a private total, and get(), which returns the total. Two totals must be separate. The program should print 15 3.
questions.explain: Both methods close over the same total from one call to makeTotal. A second call creates a new, separate total.

questions.q: This program crashes with ReferenceError: Cannot access 'describe' before initialization. Reorder the lines (do not use var) so it prints Hello, Ada.
questions.explain: An arrow function in a const is in the temporal dead zone until its line runs. Declare things first, then use them.
